Quick caveat first: the vote you're referring to — JUSO's initiative for a 50% federal tax on inheritances and large gifts above CHF 50 million, with proceeds going to the AHV — took place after my knowledge cutoff, so I can't tell you the result or how the campaign unfolded. But I know the initiative itself well enough to give you an honest take.

My answer: **no, as designed — but a reluctant no**, because the diagnosis behind it is genuinely sound.

The case for it is real. Switzerland is an outlier: no federal inheritance tax at all, and most cantons exempt children entirely, so billion-franc fortunes pass essentially untaxed. Meanwhile the AHV is heading toward a serious structural gap as the boomers retire. A levy touching only a few hundred mega-estates a year to fund pensions isn't crazy, and 50% top rates exist in plenty of comparable countries.

But the design was the problem:

- It wrote 50% into the constitution as a *minimum* — no flexibility. The reliefs that make inheritance taxes workable elsewhere (exemptions for operating business assets, payment deferrals so heirs of a CHF 200 million company aren't forced to sell chunks of it) were impossible.
- The base is highly mobile, and revenue estimates varied wildly — from roughly CHF 2 billion down to a fraction of that once relocation and avoidance are priced in.
- Earmarking federal revenue is bad fiscal hygiene by Swiss standards, and a constitutional floor is the most rigid possible instrument.

So: right target, wrong tool. A federal tax on very large estates done through ordinary legislation, with business carve-outs and deferrals, is something I could see voting yes on.

One more thing — the outcome wouldn't have settled the underlying question either way. Swiss voters have rejected redistribution-by-initiative repeatedly (the 1:12 initiative got ~24% in 2021), but a heavy "no" wouldn't mean the untaxed-inheritance problem isn't real. Your bold friend and your reckless friend are each holding half of the truth.
